title: Example Outline: Technical Article
body:
# Example Outline: ML Recommendation Systems Article

This worked example shows a complete, schema-compliant outline.json for the article defined in G-EXMP-001. Every field is populated with realistic values. Use this as a reference when producing or evaluating outlines.

---

```json
{
  "title": "When to Use Machine Learning Recommendations (And When Not To)",
  "document_type": "article",
  "domain": "general",
  "brief_id": "BRIEF-001",
  "target_word_count": 1200,
  "style_pack": "baseline-general",
  "sections": [
    {
      "id": "S1",
      "title": "The Recommendation System Decision",
      "purpose": "Frame the decision the reader is actually making, so they know whether this article applies to them.",
      "required_content": [
        "The two wrong ways to approach this decision: copying what large platforms do, and avoiding ML entirely because it seems complex",
        "The actual question: does your data volume and product stage justify the overhead?",
        "A concrete signal: products with fewer than 1,000 active users should not build ML recommendation systems yet"
      ],
      "scope_notes": "Do not define the algorithm types here — that is S2. Do not cover evaluation metrics — that is S5.",
      "estimated_word_count": 150,
      "subsections": []
    },
    {
      "id": "S2",
      "title": "Three Approaches and What They Actually Require",
      "purpose": "Give the reader a working model of the three main approaches at a level of detail sufficient to make an evaluation decision.",
      "required_content": [
        "Collaborative filtering: how it works (user-item matrix), what data it needs (interaction history), what it cannot do (new users, new items)",
        "Content-based filtering: how it works (item features), what data it needs (rich item metadata), its failure mode (filter bubbles)",
        "Hybrid approaches: when they make sense, approximate data and engineering requirements, why they are overkill for most early-stage products"
      ],
      "scope_notes": "No math. No algorithm names beyond what a PM needs to know. Do not compare specific libraries.",
      "estimated_word_count": 350,
      "subsections": [
        {
          "id": "S2.1",
          "title": "Collaborative Filtering",
          "purpose": "Explain the approach, data requirement, and cold start failure mode.",
          "required_content": ["User-item interaction data volume requirement", "Cold start problem definition"],
          "scope_notes": "No matrix factorization math.",
          "estimated_word_count": 120,
          "subsections": []
        },
        {
          "id": "S2.2",
          "title": "Content-Based Filtering",
          "purpose": "Explain the approach, metadata requirements, and filter bubble failure mode.",
          "required_content": ["Item metadata depth requirement", "Filter bubble problem definition"],
          "scope_notes": "Do not compare to collaborative filtering directly here — that is S3.",
          "estimated_word_count": 120,
          "subsections": []
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "S3",
      "title": "Choosing the Right Approach for Your Stage",
      "purpose": "Give the reader a decision framework they can apply to their actual product context.",
      "required_content": [
        "Stage 0 (under 1,000 MAU): explicit curated lists beat any algorithm",
        "Stage 1 (1,000–50,000 MAU): content-based is achievable; collaborative requires careful cold start handling",
        "Stage 2 (50,000+ MAU): hybrid becomes worthwhile; dedicated ML engineering required",
        "The single most important prerequisite: clean, consistent interaction logging before any algorithm is built"
      ],
      "scope_notes": "Do not cover evaluation here — that is S5. Do not recommend specific tools.",
      "estimated_word_count": 300,
      "subsections": []
    },
    {
      "id": "S4",
      "title": "The Three Failure Modes That Kill Recommendation Systems",
      "purpose": "Inoculate the reader against the most common implementation mistakes.",
      "required_content": [
        "Cold start: why it happens and how products typically mishandle it",
        "Popularity bias: why naive collaborative filtering just recommends the same top-10 items to everyone",
        "Feedback loops: how acting on recommendations changes the data that trains the next recommendations"
      ],
      "scope_notes": "Each failure mode is practical, not theoretical. Focus on how to detect it in production, not the algorithmic cause.",
      "estimated_word_count": 250,
      "subsections": []
    },
    {
      "id": "S5",
      "title": "How to Know If It Is Working",
      "purpose": "Give the reader concrete evaluation approaches so they can hold their engineering team accountable.",
      "required_content": [
        "Offline metrics (precision@k, recall@k) — what they measure and their limitations",
        "Online metrics (CTR, conversion lift, session depth) — why these are what actually matter",
        "The A/B test baseline: why you need a non-ML control group even after launch"
      ],
      "scope_notes": "Do not go deeper than a PM-level explanation. No metric formulas.",
      "estimated_word_count": 150,
      "subsections": []
    }
  ]
}
```

---

**What makes this outline good:** Every section has a single reader-facing purpose. No two sections overlap in scope — scope_notes explicitly declare boundaries. The required_content entries are specific enough that a section-drafter cannot miss them. Word counts sum to 1,200 words, matching the brief target. Section sequence follows the reader's comprehension needs: orient → understand options → choose → avoid mistakes → evaluate.
